name: Archetype: NATO-model armies (1945-91), Active Defense to AirLand Battle

weightNotes.aggression: In Europe the posture was defensive (forward defence of West Germany; FM 100-5 1976 'Active Defense' was criticised for prioritising defence, TRADOC history). Elsewhere Western armies attacked: Inchon 1950, Falklands 1982, Desert Storm 1991. Average 0.5.
weightNotes.maneuver: 1976 Active Defense leaned on firepower and force ratios (TRADOC history); 1982/86 FM 100-5 shifted to manoeuvre with tenets initiative, depth, agility and synchronization. 0.65 averages the era, weighted to its end.
weightNotes.flanking: AirLand Battle sought to strike the enemy's flanks and rear and attack second echelons in depth; Inchon 1950 and the 1991 left hook are the canonical examples.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Doctrine aimed at the enemy's forces and follow-on echelons, not cities; urban fighting (Hue 1968) was incidental. Low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: NATO corps sectors kept armoured counterattack reserves behind a covering force and main battle area; middling.
weightNotes.scouting: Armoured cavalry regiments, air reconnaissance, SIGINT and, late in the era, JSTARS and satellite imagery; better than Warsaw Pact ISR.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Active Defense explicitly traded space for time with units falling back between battle positions; democracies' casualty sensitivity after Vietnam. 0.2, below breakpoints.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Tank-mechanised infantry-artillery teams with close air support; AirLand Battle formalised air-ground integration (FM 100-5 1982).
weightNotes.initiative: FM 100-5 1982: commanders 'must encourage initiative in their subordinates'; German Auftragstaktik heritage in the Bundeswehr and British mission command. Uneven across NATO armies, so 0.7.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Heavy, well-resourced logistics with prepositioned stocks (POMCUS) and REFORGER; Desert Storm paused for a large logistics build-up before the ground war. High.

summary: Professional or long-service conscript armies (US, UK, West Germany, France, Israel as a close cousin) built to defeat a numerically superior Warsaw Pact. From 1976 the US Active Defense fought from successive battle positions with superior anti-tank firepower, trading space for time; from 1982 AirLand Battle added deep attack on enemy second echelons, manoeuvre against flanks and rear, and tight air-ground integration. Outside Europe the same armies conducted amphibious landings, strategic bombing campaigns and limited wars.
whyItWorked: Quality over quantity: better training, junior leadership and technology (thermal sights, attack helicopters, precision munitions late in the era) and air superiority. Desert Storm 1991, the doctrine's only full test against a Soviet-equipped army, destroyed the Iraqi army in about 100 hours of ground war. Israel 1967 and 1973 (after the first days) show the same model beating Soviet-model forces.
whereItFailed: Vietnam 1965-73: a conventional, firepower-heavy approach could not defeat a political insurgency backed by a regular army (Krepinevich, The Army and Vietnam); attrition by body count failed. Korea 1950: unprepared US units were routed by the North Korean offensive and then surprised by Chinese intervention at the Chongchon and Chosin. Its central-front promise was never tested against the Warsaw Pact.
